pages.title: Knowledge
pages.description: Notes on the systems underneath everything, written down so I don't have to relearn them.

children.title: Golang
children.description: Slices, maps and channels in memory, the GMP scheduler, goroutine leaks, and profiling with pprof.

children.title: Profiling
children.description: Measuring where a Go program spends CPU, memory and waiting time, instead of guessing, with a worked example on planear.

children.title: Garbage Collector
children.description: How Go finds and frees heap objects nothing points to, when a cycle runs, and how it differs from GCs in other languages.

children.title: Stack and Heap
children.description: Where a Go value lives, how a stack frame is laid out, and how the compiler decides stack or heap.

children.title: Cloud
children.description: Managing infrastructure as code, shipping it through CI/CD, and scheduling workloads across clusters.

children.title: Everything as Code
children.description: Why clickops can't scale, a history of as-code tools, and how to pick between push and pull reconcile.
quotes: Declarative or procedural depends on the execution domain.

children.title: Configuration Management
children.description: Configuration management keeps machines in a defined state. However, the steps to achieve such is often imperative: installing packages, configuration files and services.
quotes: Configuration management should be procedural.

children.title: Infrastructure Provisioning
children.description: Infrastructure as code declares resources (VPC, IAM, managed databases, resources) and lets an engine create, update and delete them through the provider's API.
quotes: Infrastructure as code should be declarative.
For mission-critical infra, I want a receipt of success.

children.title: OS
children.description: How the Linux kernel runs processes, from boot, devices, memory and I/O to concurrency, virtualization and latency tuning.

children.title: Command Line
children.description: Shell expansion, quoting, regular expressions, and the text tools find, grep, sed and awk, shown by example.

children.title: Kernel Fundamentals
children.description: The privilege boundary, per-process address spaces, and the path from file descriptor to disk.

children.title: Sockets
children.description: What the kernel holds for a connection before and after accept(), and how epoll lets one thread wait on many sockets.
quotes: Everything in Unix is a file descriptor.
What happens if we remove a file’s inode entry while the process keeps running?
From Kernel perspective, what’s most important when establishing TCP connection?
Why Apache Prefork is unscalable.

children.title: Devices
children.description: What devices are, how the CPU gives them work and gets results back, and where drivers fit in.
quotes: Why devices use DMA and is it even safe?
One NIC, many cores: receive side scaling (RSS)
If every device speak their own language, how does the kernel know how to interact with them?

children.title: Boot Process
children.description: From power-on to PID 1: firmware, GRUB, kernel, initramfs, systemd.
quotes: What runs before any OS?
How does the kernel get into memory?
What must the kernel do before any process exists?
Why does the kernel need a temporary root filesystem?
Adding custom module or file to initramfs.
What does PID 1 do?

children.title: Kernel and User Space
children.description: Privilege modes, syscalls, interrupts and signals: how control crosses into the kernel and back.
quotes: The kernel is not a process.
PID 1 in a container ignores any signal it has no handler for.

children.title: Memory
children.description: A deep dive into how the Linux kernel manages memory: from a virtual address to a physical page frame, and when the kernel comes in to resolve missing mappings.
quotes: Why share the kernel half in every PGD?
Is a page table entry sufficient in fully describing the page frame?
Are page table entries and page frames sufficient for new process memory addressing?
COW is essentially the case where the PTE is stricter than what VMA says.

children.title: Files and I/O
children.description: How a filesystem is laid out on disk, how it survives a power cut, and how the kernel rebuilds it in memory.
quotes: Common mistake: why can't I open anything in a directory I can “read”?
Setting umask sets default values for processes to use when creating files / directories.
Where on the disk does a filesystem live?
Can one block device be built out of others?
What if a filesystem outgrows its partition?
To determine what goes into the disk, reason what must survive a power cut.
What if power to disk cuts mid-update?
How does a name find its data?
Loopback device: mounting a file as a disk.
How does the kernel rebuild this in memory?
What does a lookup cost?
What's behind each top-level directory?
Daniel’s Filesystem Office: does du always equal df?

children.title: Concurrency
children.description: Why would we ever need concurrency / parallelization? In this page, we will dive into the 3 use cases that calls for concurrency in modern technology.
quotes: CPU performance bottleneck reached (~2005)
Did software become increasingly parallel naturally or due to hardware constraints?
Did modern services become more sluggish with the shift to microservices?

children.title: Process vs Thread
children.description: A fundamental breakdown of the architecture of processes and OS threads in the kernel.

children.title: GMP Scheduler
children.description: The best practical implementation of coroutines: how Go multiplexes goroutines onto OS threads using GMP scheduler model.
quotes: Why other languages absolutely suck at coroutines.
Set GOMAXPROCS to num cores (default)

children.title: Low-Latency Tuning
children.description: Trading throughput and power for predictable latency: NUMA, hugepages, C-states, CPU isolation and busy polling.
quotes: RHEL applies these settings as one

children.title: Virtualization
children.description: Utilization is the real goal; isolation and hardware decoupling are what let workloads bin-pack safely onto one box.
quotes: Is virtualization really synonymous with “isolation” and “division”?
When to use a VM over containers?
My experience with Pet vs Herd Kubernetes clusters.
How we achieved binpacking in Bytedance Kubernetes clusters

children.title: Containerization
children.description: How kubelet's request becomes a running container process, and why each piece in the chain exists.
quotes: Does kubelet really stop your container, or are zombies left behind?

children.title: Namespaces
children.description: What a container can see: per-process copies of kernel resource tables, namespace types, and rootless user namespaces.

children.title: cgroups
children.description: Per-group resource limits written as files: cgroup v1 versus v2, Docker flags, Kubernetes QoS, and eBPF.

children.title: Virtual Machines
children.description: KVM and QEMU memory mapping, Firecracker's fast boot path, and emulated, virtio, VFIO and SR-IOV devices.
quotes: Deep dive into the some history about VMs.
RHEL and VMware’s interesting frenemy relationship.
How can we stop devices with DMA from touching memory outside its assigned VM?

children.title: Network
children.description: The network stack from DNS, HTTP and TLS in userspace down to TCP, routing and the NIC.
quotes: What is the true defintion of the OSI model?
The OSI textbook layer does not provide a perfect normative direction for creating modern network stacks.
Instead, we should think in terms of execution boundaries.

children.title: Linux Networking
children.description: What a Linux host does with packets beyond being an endpoint: forwarding modes, netfilter, container networking and the packet path.

children.title: Container Networking
children.description: How a pod gets its network: veth pairs, CNI plugins, and how Services reach pods through kube-proxy.

children.title: Netfilter and conntrack
children.description: How Linux filters and NATs packets: netfilter hooks, iptables and nftables, and connection tracking.

children.title: Bridging, Routing and NAT
children.description: Three ways a VM reaches the network, judged by the source address the home router sees.

children.title: Packet Path and Kernel Bypass
children.description: NIC ring buffers, softirq and NAPI, where latency creeps in, and skipping the kernel with DPDK and RDMA.

children.title: Link (Fabric)
children.description: Delivery inside a LAN or data centre: ARP, DHCP, VLANs, spanning tree and leaf-spine fabrics with VXLAN and EVPN.

children.title: VXLAN and EVPN
children.description: VXLAN extends a layer-2 segment across a routed fabric by encapsulating Ethernet frames in UDP/IP. BGP EVPN is its control plane: it advertises the VTEP behind each MAC and IP address.
quotes: What problem does VXLAN fundamentally solve?
Why does VXLAN need a control plane?

children.title: Leaf-Spine and ECMP
children.description: How data centres moved from Spanning Tree trees to routed leaf-spine fabrics, and how ECMP keeps every link in use.
quotes: Why did three-tier stop fitting?

children.title: Spanning Tree
children.description: How STP breaks layer-2 loops, why it wastes links and converges slowly, and what replaced it.
quotes: Why does Ethernet need STP?
Why not just tune STP's timers?

children.title: ARP and DHCP
children.description: Resolving a neighbour's MAC with ARP, leasing an address through DHCP's DORA exchange, and defending both against spoofing.

children.title: VLAN
children.description: Splitting one switched network into broadcast domains: when hosts need a router, trunking, VLAN assignment and 802.1Q tags.

children.title: Network (Router)
children.description: Source-to-destination delivery across networks: addressing, ICMP, NAT, routing protocols, MPLS and VPNs.

children.title: VPNs
children.description: Tunnelling private traffic across the internet with IPsec and WireGuard.

children.title: Routing
children.description: How routers build their tables: OSPF inside one AS, BGP between ASes, and fast failover.
quotes: Why does a router need administrative distance?
Why can't the internet run as one ginormous OSPF network?
Why do we need iBGP?
Why is iBGP ranked below OSPF?

children.title: Internet Structure
children.description: How ISPs connect through transit, peering and IXPs, and how to carve address space with CIDR and VLSM.

children.title: IP Options and ICMP
children.description: Record and source route options, how ICMP reports errors back to the source, and how ping and traceroute use it.

children.title: NAT and NAT Traversal
children.description: How NAT shares one public address, why symmetric NATs break hole punching, and the ways back in: port forwarding, TURN and ICE.

children.title: MPLS
children.description: Forwarding on short per-link labels instead of a longest-prefix match, and what that buys: traffic engineering, VPNs and QoS.

children.title: Reaching google.com
children.description: Every step of loading google.com: DNS, TCP handshake, load balancers, CDNs, anycast, TLS and HTTP.

children.title: Application (Userspace)
children.description: Protocols the application owns and debugs itself: DNS, HTTP, TLS, load balancing and P2P.

children.title: Load Balancing
children.description: L4 vs L7 load balancing, direct server return, and consistent hashing.

children.title: HTTP
children.description: HTTP/1.0 through HTTP/3 compared on transport, head-of-line blocking, binary framing, and HPACK and QPACK header compression.

children.title: TLS
children.description: The TLS handshake, what a certificate signature proves, how clients verify chains, which CA to choose, and lookup tables for errors, trust stores and openssl.
quotes: Known issues with the current

children.title: DNS
children.description: Resolution through root, TLD and authoritative servers, delegation versus forwarding with dig and dnsmasq, the wire format, and DNSSEC versus DoH.

children.title: P2P and BitTorrent
children.description: Why P2P distribution scales with its peers, how BitTorrent picks pieces and rewards uploaders with tit-for-tat, plus IPFS and Usenet.

children.title: Transport (Host)
children.description: Process-to-process delivery as the host kernel executes it: the socket interface and TCP.

children.title: TCP
children.description: Connection setup and teardown, TIME-WAIT, Nagle and delayed ACK, and congestion control from Reno to BBR.

children.title: Socket Programming
children.description: TCP and UDP call sequences in Python and C, iterative versus concurrent servers, framing a byte stream, and raw sockets.

children.title: Debugging
children.description: Common network error messages by layer, quick diagnostic commands, and first steps in an incident.

children.title: Encapsulation and Decapsulation
children.description: What each layer adds on the way down: TCP, UDP, IPv4 and Ethernet header fields, fragmentation and path MTU discovery.

pages.title: Homelab
pages.description: My self-hosted lab: what runs on it, how it's wired, and why.

children.title: OIDC
children.description: How OIDC sign-in works, and how Authelia signs in Outline, Kaneo, Komodo and OpenBao with hashed client secrets.

children.title: Groups and Access
children.description: Authentik roles, per-app grant groups and invitations that decide who can open each self-hosted app.

children.title: Architecture
children.description: Management, services and lab zones, the three homelab repos, and off-site backups to S3.

children.title: Networking
children.description: NAT on the hypervisor, the three VM bridge subnets, and Tailscale subnet routing for remote access.

children.title: DNS
children.description: Pi-hole as the lab resolver, with forwards to Consul and br-lab, and Cloudflare for public names.

children.title: Config as Code
children.description: Why I chose Ansible, and how Ansible, Komodo and Windmill split the homelab between three git repos.

children.title: Ansible
children.description: Agentless Ansible over SSH for my hypervisor and VMs: playbooks, inventory, making changes and bootstrap.

children.title: Disaster Recovery
children.description: Restic backups to S3 for Postgres, Komodo's MongoDB, app volumes and lab VMs, with schedules and retention.

children.title: Services
children.description: Which Compose projects run on each VM, and how databases, secrets, Consul discovery and login are wired.
